claim: The Drosophila ventral nerve cord (VNC) is composed of thousands of neurons born from a set of individually identifiable stem cells.
source: The Drosophila ventral nerve cord (VNC) is composed of thousands of neurons born from a set of individually identifiable stem cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about VNC organization that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Unc-4 functions in lineage 11A to promote cholinergic neurotransmitter identity and suppress the GABA fate.
source: We found that Unc-4 functions in lineage 11A to promote cholinergic neurotransmitter identity and suppress the GABA fate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing ectopic GABAergic neurons in 11A lineage in unc-4 mutants (Figure 4D-K) and RNA in situ hybridization results.

claim: In lineage 7B, Unc-4 promotes proper neuronal projections to the leg neuropil.
source: In lineage 7B, Unc-4 promotes proper neuronal projections to the leg neuropil and a specific flight-related take-off behavior.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data showing reduced 7B projections to leg neuropils in unc-4 mutants (Figures 5A, 6C-I).

claim: In lineage 7B, Unc-4 promotes a specific flight-related take-off behavior.
source: In lineage 7B, Unc-4 promotes proper neuronal projections to the leg neuropil and a specific flight-related take-off behavior.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing interrupted take-off behavior in 7B-specific unc-4 knockouts (Figure 7, Videos 13-15).

claim: Unc-4 acts peripherally to promote proprioceptive sensory organ development.
source: We also uncovered that Unc-4 acts peripherally to promote proprioceptive sensory organ development and the execution of specific leg-related behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by data showing disrupted organization of femoral chordotonal organ neurons in unc-4 mutants (Figure 3J-M).

claim: Unc-4 acts peripherally to promote the execution of specific leg-related behaviors.
source: We also uncovered that Unc-4 acts peripherally to promote proprioceptive sensory organ development and the execution of specific leg-related behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing defects in climbing, walking, and three-leg rubbing when Unc-4 is removed from chordotonal lineage (Table 1, Figure 3I, Videos 10-12).

claim: Unc-4 function is required during development, but not in the adult, to regulate neuronal identity and behavior.
source: Through time-dependent conditional knock-out of Unc-4, we found that its function is required during development, but not in the adult, to regulate the above events.
evidence: This is supported by TARGET system experiments showing that early embryonic removal of Unc-4 causes behavioral defects, but late pupal removal does not.

claim: The adult Drosophila VNC manifests a lineage-based organization similar to the vertebrate spinal cord.
source: The adult Drosophila ventral nerve cord (VNC), like the vertebrate spinal cord, also manifests a lineage-based organization.
evidence: This is a comparative statement drawing on established knowledge about both systems.

claim: The cellular complexity of the VNC arises from a set of segmentally repeated set of 30 paired and one unpaired neural stem cells (Neuroblasts [NBs]).
source: The cellular complexity of the VNC arises from a set of segmentally repeated set of 30 paired and one unpaired neural stem cells (Neuroblasts [NBs]), which arise at stereotypic locations during early development (Doe, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work (Doe, 1992).

claim: NBs undergo two major phases of proliferation: the embryonic phase and the post-embryonic phase.
source: These individually identifiable NBs undergo two major phases of proliferation: the embryonic phase generates the functional neurons of the larval CNS, some of which are remodeled to function in the adult, and the post-embryonic phase generates most of the adult neurons (Truman and Bate, 1988; Truman, 1990; Prokop and Technau, 1991; Bossing et al., 1996; Schmid et al., 1999; Consoulas et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Each NB generates a secondary precursor cell, which divides via Notch-mediated asymmetric cell division to generate two neurons with distinct identities.
source: Each NB generates a secondary precursor cell, which divides via Notch-mediated asymmetric cell division to generate two neurons with distinct identities (Spana and Doe, 1996; Skeath and Doe, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Spana and Doe, 1996; Skeath and Doe, 1998).

claim: Each NB produces two distinct hemilineages of neurons, termed Notch-ON or the 'A' and Notch-OFF or the 'B' hemilineage.
source: After many rounds of such cell divisions, each NB ends up producing two distinct hemilineages of neurons, termed Notch-ON or the 'A' and Notch-OFF or the 'B' hemilineage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VNC development based on prior work.

claim: Within a hemilineage, neurons acquire similar fates based on transcription factor expression, neurotransmitter usage, and axonal projection.
source: Within a hemilineage, neurons acquire similar fates based on transcription factor expression, neurotransmitter usage, and axonal projection (Truman et al., 2010; Lacin et al., 2014; Lacin et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work including authors' own publications.

claim: Neurons of each hemilineage appear dedicated for specific behaviors.
source: Moreover, neurons of each hemilineage appear dedicated for specific behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by examples cited in the following sentence and references to prior work.

claim: Artificial neuronal activation of the glutamatergic hemilineage 2A neurons elicit specifically high frequency wing beating.
source: For example, artificial neuronal activation of the glutamatergic hemilineage 2A neurons elicit specifically high frequency wing beating, while the same treatment of the cholinergic hemilineage 7B neurons leads to a specific take-off behavior (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2015.

claim: Artificial neuronal activation of the cholinergic hemilineage 7B neurons leads to a specific take-off behavior.
source: For example, artificial neuronal activation of the glutamatergic hemilineage 2A neurons elicit specifically high frequency wing beating, while the same treatment of the cholinergic hemilineage 7B neurons leads to a specific take-off behavior (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2015.

claim: Hemilineages represent the fundamental developmental and functional unit of the VNC.
source: Thus, hemilineages represent the fundamental developmental and functional unit of the VNC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the evidence presented in the preceding sentences about hemilineage organization and function.

claim: Unc-4 is an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional repressor.
source: Unc-4, an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional repressor, is expressed post-mitotically in seven of the 14 cholinergic hemilineages in the VNC: three 'A' -Notch-ON- hemilineages (11A, 12A, and 17A) and four 'B' -Notch-OFF- hemilineages (7B, 18B, 19B, and 23B) (Miller et al., 1992; Rovescalli et al., 1996; Lacin et al., 2014; Lacin et al., 2019; Nittoli et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Miller et al., 1992; Rovescalli et al., 1996; Lacin et al., 2014; Lacin et al., 2019; Nittoli et al., 2019).

claim: Unc-4 is expressed post-mitotically in seven of the 14 cholinergic hemilineages in the VNC: three 'A' hemilineages (11A, 12A, and 17A) and four 'B' hemilineages (7B, 18B, 19B, and 23B).
source: Unc-4, an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional repressor, is expressed post-mitotically in seven of the 14 cholinergic hemilineages in the VNC: three 'A' -Notch-ON- hemilineages (11A, 12A, and 17A) and four 'B' -Notch-OFF- hemilineages (7B, 18B, 19B, and 23B) (Miller et al., 1992; Rovescalli et al., 1996; Lacin et al., 2014; Lacin et al., 2019; Nittoli et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work including authors' own publications.

claim: For four of the Unc-4+ hemilineages (7B, 17A, 18B, and 23B), the neurons of the sibling hemilineage undergo cell death.
source: For four of the Unc-4+ hemilineages (7B, 17A, 18B, and 23B), the neurons of the sibling hemilineage undergo cell death (Truman et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Truman et al., 2010.

claim: For three Unc-4+ hemilineages (11A, 12A, and 19B), the neurons of the sibling hemilineage are GABAergic.
source: For the remaining three (11A, 12A, and 19B), the neurons of the sibling hemilineage are GABAergic (Lacin et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lacin et al., 2019.

claim: Unc-4 expression in these hemilineages is restricted to postmitotic neurons and it appears to mark uniformly all neurons within a hemilineage during development and adult life.
source: Unc-4 expression in these hemilineages is restricted to postmitotic neurons and it appears to mark uniformly all neurons within a hemilineage during development and adult life (Lacin et al., 2014; Lacin and Truman, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Lacin et al., 2014; Lacin and Truman, 2016).

claim: The unc-4null mutant line lacks the homeodomain.
source: To generate the unc-4null mutant line, we used Flippase (FLP) to excise the 2nd and 3rd exons of unc-4 in the germline, generating an unc-4 allele that lacks the homeodomain (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design described and confirmed by molecular analysis and immunostaining (Figure 1B,C).

claim: Molecular analysis confirmed the presence of the expected deletion in unc-4null mutant.
source: Molecular analysis confirmed the presence of the expected deletion and immunostainings revealed no detectable protein expression in the unc-4null mutant (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by molecular analysis data and immunostaining results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Immunostainings revealed no detectable Unc-4 protein expression in the unc-4null mutant.
source: Molecular analysis confirmed the presence of the expected deletion and immunostainings revealed no detectable protein expression in the unc-4null mutant (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C comparing control and mutant embryos.

claim: Unc-4 is expressed in all progenitors of leg chordotonal neurons (sensory organ precursors [SOPs]).
source: Leveraging these transgenes, we tracked Unc-4 expression in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) and found that Unc-4 is expressed in all progenitors of leg chordotonal neurons (also called sensory organ precursors [SOPs]) and head sense organs in the larvae as well as many adult sensory neurons including chordotonal and bristle sensory neurons in the leg and Johnston's organ and olfactory neurons in the antenna (Figure 1G–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1G-H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unc-4 is expressed in head sense organs in the larvae.
source: Leveraging these transgenes, we tracked Unc-4 expression in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) and found that Unc-4 is expressed in all progenitors of leg chordotonal neurons (also called sensory organ precursors [SOPs]) and head sense organs in the larvae as well as many adult sensory neurons including chordotonal and bristle sensory neurons in the leg and Johnston's organ and olfactory neurons in the antenna (Figure 1G–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1G-H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unc-4 is expressed in many adult sensory neurons including chordotonal and bristle sensory neurons in the leg.
source: Leveraging these transgenes, we tracked Unc-4 expression in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) and found that Unc-4 is expressed in all progenitors of leg chordotonal neurons (also called sensory organ precursors [SOPs]) and head sense organs in the larvae as well as many adult sensory neurons including chordotonal and bristle sensory neurons in the leg and Johnston's organ and olfactory neurons in the antenna (Figure 1G–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unc-4 is expressed in Johnston's organ and olfactory neurons in the antenna.
source: Leveraging these transgenes, we tracked Unc-4 expression in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) and found that Unc-4 is expressed in all progenitors of leg chordotonal neurons (also called sensory organ precursors [SOPs]) and head sense organs in the larvae as well as many adult sensory neurons including chordotonal and bristle sensory neurons in the leg and Johnston's organ and olfactory neurons in the antenna (Figure 1G–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NB7-4 specific FLP expression in the unc-4FRT larva removes Unc-4 expression from the 23B neurons but not the 7B neurons.
source: This manipulation resulted in loss of Unc-4 expression specifically in 23B neurons, but no other lineage (Figure 1I), highlighting the ability of our system to ablate Unc-4 function in a lineage specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1I demonstrating lineage-specific removal.

claim: All loss of function unc-4 alleles exhibited semi-lethality in the hemizygous or homozygous state.
source: All loss of function unc-4 alleles we generated (null, AD, DBD, and GAL4) exhibited semi-lethality in the hemizygous or homozygous state, with many pharate adults failing to eclose from the pupal case.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data on survival rates of mutant flies.

claim: Escaper unc-4 null flies emerged as adults with a frequency of 13% of the expected Mendelian rate.
source: Escaper unc-4 null flies emerged as adults with a frequency of 13% of the expected Mendelian rate.
evidence: This is quantitative data from survival experiments shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Adult unc-4 null mutant males were fertile, but females were infertile.
source: Adult unc-4 null mutant males were fertile, but females were infertile.
evidence: This is an observation from fertility experiments with mutant flies.

claim: unc-4 mutant females were impaired in egg laying and their ovaries were dramatically enlarged due to egg retention.
source: Examination of unc-4 females revealed that they were impaired in egg laying and their ovaries were dramatically enlarged due to egg retention (not shown), a phenotype that may arise due to defective functioning of sensory neurons in the female reproductive tract, some of which express Unc-4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from examination of mutant females, with speculation about the cause.

claim: All unc-4 mutant animals manifested erect wings.
source: All unc-4 mutant animals manifested erect wings, and none could fly or jump (Figure 2A,C,I; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations and quantification shown in Figure 2A,I and Video 1.

claim: No unc-4 mutant animals could fly or jump.
source: All unc-4 mutant animals manifested erect wings, and none could fly or jump (Figure 2A,C,I; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations and quantification shown in Figure 2C,I and Video 1.

claim: unc-4 mutant adults could walk but only in an uncoordinated manner.
source: unc-4 mutant adults could walk but only in an uncoordinated manner as most failed a climbing assay (see methods) due to falling or being extremely slow (Figure 2G,I; Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations shown in Figure 2G,I and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: Most unc-4 mutants failed a climbing assay due to falling or being extremely slow.
source: unc-4 mutant adults could walk but only in an uncoordinated manner as most failed a climbing assay (see methods) due to falling or being extremely slow (Figure 2G,I; Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2I and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: unc-4 mutants showed impaired grooming due to lack of coordination among legs.
source: unc-4 mutants also showed impaired grooming due to lack of coordination among legs, and they completely failed in executing three-leg rubbing (Figure 2E,I; Video 4), a characteristic behavior which requires coordination of three legs for cleaning (Phillis et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations shown in Figure 2E,I and Video 4.

claim: unc-4 mutants completely failed in executing three-leg rubbing.
source: unc-4 mutants also showed impaired grooming due to lack of coordination among legs, and they completely failed in executing three-leg rubbing (Figure 2E,I; Video 4), a characteristic behavior which requires coordination of three legs for cleaning (Phillis et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2I and Video 4.

claim: Three-leg rubbing is a characteristic behavior which requires coordination of three legs for cleaning.
source: unc-4 mutants also showed impaired grooming due to lack of coordination among legs, and they completely failed in executing three-leg rubbing (Figure 2E,I; Video 4), a characteristic behavior which requires coordination of three legs for cleaning (Phillis et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Phillis et al., 1993.

claim: unc-4DBD-tubAD driven unc-4 expression rescued the observed behavioral defects as well as the semilethality.
source: unc-4DBD-tubAD driven unc-4 expression rescued the observed behavioral defects as well as the semilethality (Figure 2B,D,F,H; Videos 2–6).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2B,D,F,H,I and Videos 2-6.

claim: Rescued unc-4 animals were still slow to take-off compared to wild type.
source: These rescued animals, however, did not behave like wild type: they were still slow to take-off (Video 6) and still exhibited defects in three-leg rubbing (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral analysis shown in Video 6.

claim: Rescued unc-4 animals still exhibited defects in three-leg rubbing.
source: These rescued animals, however, did not behave like wild type: they were still slow to take-off (Video 6) and still exhibited defects in three-leg rubbing (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral analysis.

claim: A BAC transgene containing the unc-4 locus rescued essentially 100% of all observed phenotypes in unc-4 mutant flies.
source: To ensure that all observed defects were the result of loss of Unc-4 function, we introduced a BAC transgene that contains the unc-4 locus (Venken et al., 2010) into unc-4 mutant flies and observed essentially 100% rescue of all observed phenotypes (Figure 2I; also compare Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2I and Videos 6 and 7.

claim: Unc-4 function is required for take-off, flight, climbing and grooming behaviors.
source: Our findings, thus, clearly show that Unc-4 function is required for take-off, flight, climbing and grooming behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral defects observed in unc-4 mutants and their rescue.

claim: Early embryonic removal of Unc-4 resulted in the same behavioral defects as seen in unc-4 mutants.
source: We observed that early embryonic removal of Unc-4 resulted in the same behavioral defects as seen in unc-4 mutants, but its removal in late pupal stages yielded flies that behaved like wild-type (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by TARGET system experiments with temporal control of Unc-4 removal.

claim: Removal of Unc-4 in late pupal stages yielded flies that behaved like wild-type.
source: We observed that early embryonic removal of Unc-4 resulted in the same behavioral defects as seen in unc-4 mutants, but its removal in late pupal stages yielded flies that behaved like wild-type (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by TARGET system experiments with temporal control of Unc-4 removal.

claim: Unc-4 functions during development to regulate specific behaviors.
source: Unc-4, therefore, functions during development to regulate this suite of specific behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal removal experiments showing developmental requirement.

claim: sca-GAL4 removed most Unc-4 expression from the CNS.
source: sca-GAL4 removed most Unc-4 expression from the CNS, all of Unc-4 expression from the progenitors of chordotonal sense organs, and also Unc-4 expression in epithelial cells of the leg disc (Figure 3B,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B,F.

claim: sca-GAL4 removed all of Unc-4 expression from the progenitors of chordotonal sense organs.
source: sca-GAL4 removed most Unc-4 expression from the CNS, all of Unc-4 expression from the progenitors of chordotonal sense organs, and also Unc-4 expression in epithelial cells of the leg disc (Figure 3B,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: dpnEE-GAL4 removed most Unc-4 expression from the CNS but left Unc-4 expression in leg discs largely intact.
source: dpnEE-GAL4 which is expressed specifically in CNS NBs (Emery and Bier, 1995; Yang et al., 2016) removed most Unc-4 expression from the CNS but left Unc-4 expression in leg discs largely intact (Figure 3C,G).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C,G.

claim: sca-GAL4 mediated knock-out of Unc-4 function led to erect wings, failure to fly, and grooming and climbing defects.
source: sca-GAL4 mediated knock-out of Unc-4 function led to the same behavioral defects observed in unc-4 mutant animals: all had erect wings, failed to fly, and showed grooming and climbing defects (Table 1; Video 8).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Table 1 and Video 8.

claim: dpnEE-GAL4 mediated removal of Unc-4 from the CNS resulted in erect wings, inability to fly, and mild grooming defects.
source: By contrast, the dpnEE-GAL4 mediated removal from the CNS gave a partial phenotype with the flies having erect wings, an inability to fly, and mild grooming defects (Table 1), but they performed well on the climbing assay scoring at the same level as controls (Table 1; Video 9).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Table 1 and Video 9.

claim: dpnEE-GAL4 mediated removal of Unc-4 from the CNS did not impair climbing performance.
source: By contrast, the dpnEE-GAL4 mediated removal from the CNS gave a partial phenotype with the flies having erect wings, an inability to fly, and mild grooming defects (Table 1), but they performed well on the climbing assay scoring at the same level as controls (Table 1; Video 9).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Table 1 and Video 9.

claim: Unc-4 related PNS deficits are responsible for the poor climbing performance.
source: These results suggest that Unc-4 related PNS deficits are responsible for the poor climbing performance, while both PNS and CNS deficits are responsible for grooming defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from comparing sca-GAL4 and dpnEE-GAL4 mediated knockouts.

claim: Both PNS and CNS deficits are responsible for grooming defects in unc-4 mutants.
source: These results suggest that Unc-4 related PNS deficits are responsible for the poor climbing performance, while both PNS and CNS deficits are responsible for grooming defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from comparing sca-GAL4 and dpnEE-GAL4 mediated knockouts.

claim: ato-GAL4 removed Unc-4 expression completely from chordotonal lineage while leaving Unc-4 expression in the CNS intact.
source: To do this, we used a chordotonal SOP-specific driver ato-GAL4 (Hassan et al., 2000) to remove Unc-4 function completely from chordotonal lineage (progenitors and neurons), while leaving Unc-4 expression in the CNS intact (Figure 3D,H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D,H.

claim: ato-GAL4 also unexpectedly removed Unc-4 expression in the epithelial cells of most leg discs.
source: ato-GAL4 also unexpectedly removed Unc-4 expression in the epithelial cells of most leg discs (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: ato-GAL4 mediated removal of Unc-4 function resulted in coordination defects in leg movements including defects in three-leg rubbing and walking.
source: ato-GAL4 mediated removal of Unc-4 function in chordotonal lineage and epithelial cells resulted in coordination defects in leg movements: we observed defects in three-leg rubbing (Table 1; Video 10) and walking (Videos 11 and 12).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Table 1 and Videos 10-12.

claim: ato-GAL4 driven FLP expression impaired the negative-geotaxis behavior of control animals.
source: We did not assess climbing behavior of the resulting flies because ato-GAL4 driven FLP expression impaired the negative-geotaxis behavior of control animals (presumably due to ato-GAL4 expression in the gravity sensing Johnston organ or its progenitor cells).
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral experiments with speculation about the cause.

claim: Control animals walked in a coordinated manner without falling.
source: Control animals walked in a coordinated manner without falling, but unc-4 null mutants and ato-GAL4 >unc4 FRT flies were slow and fell often (Videos 11 and 12; Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations shown in Videos 11 and 12 and quantification in Figure 3I.

claim: unc-4 null mutants and ato-GAL4 >unc4 FRT flies were slow and fell often during walking.
source: Control animals walked in a coordinated manner without falling, but unc-4 null mutants and ato-GAL4 >unc4 FRT flies were slow and fell often (Videos 11 and 12; Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations shown in Videos 11 and 12 and quantification in Figure 3I.

claim: Loss of unc-4 function in the leg discs is required to drive proper leg-related behaviors, including three-leg rubbing, walking, and likely climbing.
source: Thus, our results indicate that loss of unc-4 function in the leg discs, presumably in the chordotonal lineage, is required to drive proper leg-related behaviors, including three-leg rubbing, walking, and likely climbing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ato-GAL4 mediated knockout experiments.

claim: In control animals, feCO neuronal cell bodies are clustered and located proximally near the trochanter border.
source: In control animals, feCO neuronal cell bodies are clustered and located proximally near the trochanter border; they extend dendrites in a stereotyped fashion (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: In unc-4 mutants, the cell bodies of many feCO neurons were displaced across the femur.
source: In the mutants, the cell bodies of many of the neurons were displaced across the femur (Figure 3K,L) and their bundled dendritic projections appeared to be disrupted as compared to controls; all of these defects were rescued with restored Unc-4 function (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3K,L.

claim: In unc-4 mutants, bundled dendritic projections of feCO neurons appeared to be disrupted as compared to controls.
source: In the mutants, the cell bodies of many of the neurons were displaced across the femur (Figure 3K,L) and their bundled dendritic projections appeared to be disrupted as compared to controls; all of these defects were rescued with restored Unc-4 function (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3K,L.

claim: All feCO defects in unc-4 mutants were rescued with restored Unc-4 function.
source: In the mutants, the cell bodies of many of the neurons were displaced across the femur (Figure 3K,L) and their bundled dendritic projections appeared to be disrupted as compared to controls; all of these defects were rescued with restored Unc-4 function (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Axonal projections of the FeCO neurons in the VNC of unc-4 mutant animals appeared like wild-type.
source: Of note, axonal projections of the FeCO neurons in the VNC of unc-4 mutant animals appeared like wild-type (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from imaging experiments.

claim: Unc-4 appears to regulate the patterning and dendritic projections of chordotonal neurons in the leg.
source: Unc-4, therefore, appears to regulate the patterning and dendritic projections of chordotonal neurons in the leg, with this function likely underlying the observed defects in three-leg rubbing, walking, and climbing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical defects observed in feCO neurons.

claim: Unc-4 function in chordotonal neurons likely underlies the observed defects in three-leg rubbing, walking, and climbing.
source: Unc-4, therefore, appears to regulate the patterning and dendritic projections of chordotonal neurons in the leg, with this function likely underlying the observed defects in three-leg rubbing, walking, and climbing.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the anatomical and behavioral data.

claim: Seven hemilineages that express Unc-4 are all cholinergic.
source: The central expression of Unc-4 is striking because that seven hemilineages that express it are all cholinergic (Lacin et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lacin et al., 2019.

claim: No gross defects were observed in the number and position of Unc-4+ neurons in the absence of Unc-4 function.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, we observed no gross defects in the number and position of Unc-4+ neurons in the absence of Unc-4 function, indicating Unc-4 is not required for its own expression nor is it required for the survival of these neurons.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A comparing control and mutant.

claim: Unc-4 is not required for its own expression.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, we observed no gross defects in the number and position of Unc-4+ neurons in the absence of Unc-4 function, indicating Unc-4 is not required for its own expression nor is it required for the survival of these neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Unc-4+ neurons are still present in mutants (Figure 4A).

claim: Unc-4 is not required for the survival of Unc-4+ neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, we observed no gross defects in the number and position of Unc-4+ neurons in the absence of Unc-4 function, indicating Unc-4 is not required for its own expression nor is it required for the survival of these neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Unc-4+ neurons are still present in mutants (Figure 4A).

claim: Most Unc-4+ neurons including neurons of all seven postembryonic hemilineages in the control VNC were marked with unc-4AD-ChATDBD.
source: As expected, most Unc-4+ neurons including neurons of all seven postembryonic hemilineages (identified based on location and axonal projection) in the control VNC were marked with the split-GAL4 combination of unc-4AD-ChATDBD, confirming the cholinergic identity of the Unc-4+ hemilineages.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the unc-4 mutant VNC, the expression of unc-4AD-ChATDBD appeared grossly normal and marked all seven Unc-4+ postembryonic hemilineages.
source: In the unc-4 mutant VNC, the expression of this split-GAL4 combination appeared grossly normal and marked all seven Unc-4+ postembryonic hemilineages, indicating that Unc-4 function is not necessary for the cholinergic fate of most (but not all, see below) neurons in these hemilineages.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Unc-4 function is not necessary for the cholinergic fate of most neurons in Unc-4+ hemilineages.
source: In the unc-4 mutant VNC, the expression of this split-GAL4 combination appeared grossly normal and marked all seven Unc-4+ postembryonic hemilineages, indicating that Unc-4 function is not necessary for the cholinergic fate of most (but not all, see below) neurons in these hemilineages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that ChAT expression persists in most Unc-4+ neurons in mutants.

claim: unc-4AD-VGlutDBD identified several glutamatergic Unc-4+ motor neurons in thoracic and abdominal segments.
source: Here, unc-4AD-VGlutDBD driven GFP expression identified several glutamatergic Unc-4+ motor neurons in thoracic and abdominal segments in addition to a few occasional interneurons in the thoracic segments (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Based on their axon projections, glutamatergic Unc-4+ motor neurons were the MN1-5 neurons that innervate the indirect flight muscles, as well as motoneurons to neck and haltere muscles and the abdominal body wall.
source: Based on their axon projections, these motor neurons were the MN1-5 neurons, that innervate the indirect flight muscles, as well as motoneurons to neck and haltere muscles and the abdominal body wall (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on anatomical identification using axon projection patterns shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most adult glutamatergic Unc-4+ motoneurons come from remodeled larval motoneurons.
source: Most of these adult motoneurons come from remodeled larval motoneurons (Consoulas et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Consoulas et al., 2002.

claim: Glutamatergic Unc-4+ motor neurons are remodeled versions of larval U/CQ motor neurons from NB7-1 and embryonic-born neurons from NB2-4 lineage.
source: Comparison of the adult cells with unc-4AD-VGlutDBD expression in the larval VNC indicated that these are remodeled versions of larval U/CQ motor neurons, from NB7-1 while others are likely embryonic-born neurons from NB2-4 lineage (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of larval and adult expression patterns shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the VNC of unc-4 mutant adults, glutamatergic Unc-4+ motor neurons were still present and marked with unc-4AD-VGlutDBD, but they were disorganized and reduced in size.
source: In the VNC of unc-4 mutant adults, these motor neurons were still present and marked with unc-4AD-VGlutDBD, but they were disorganized and reduced in size (Figure 4C; the MN5 size: 283+/- 54 μm2 in controls vs 94+/- 31 μm2 in mutants; N = 10 and 14 cells, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantitative morphometric data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Unc-4 is expressed in embryonic-born remodeled adult motor neurons and functions to promote their growth.
source: Unc-4, thus, is expressed in embryonic-born remodeled adult motor neurons and functions to promote their growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of reduced motor neuron size in mutants.

claim: In control animals, no GABAergic Unc-4+ neurons were detected in the VNC.
source: In control animals, we failed to detect any GABAergic Unc-4+ neurons in the VNC (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All Unc-4+ postembyonic hemilineages in the VNC express ChAT mRNA but not gad1 mRNA.
source: RNA in situ hybridization against gad1 and ChAT genes confirmed this and our previous published findings and showed that all Unc-4+ postembyonic hemilineages in the VNC express ChAT mRNA but not gad1 mRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In unc-4 mutants, unc-4DBD-gad1AD marked many neurons in the VNC.
source: In unc-4 mutants, however, unc-4DBD-gad1AD marked many neurons in the VNC (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Presence of a BAC clone containing unc-4 locus reversed the ectopic GABAergic expression pattern, significantly reducing the number of ectopic GABAergic neurons.
source: Presence of a BAC clone containing unc-4 locus reversed this expression pattern, significantly reducing the number of ectopic GABAergic neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The ectopic GABAergic neurons in unc-4 mutants are a subset of the cholinergic hemilineage 11A.
source: We identified these cells as a subset of the cholinergic hemilineage 11A (Harris et al., 2015; Lacin et al., 2019; Shepherd et al., 2019) based on the following observations: (i) like 11A neurons, they reside in posterior and dorsal region of only T1 and T2 segments (Figure 4D), (ii) their axonal trajectories match that of the 11A neurons (Figure 4F–G), (iii) they express Nkx6, a marker for 11A neurons (Figure 4H), and (iv) they intermingle with Eve+ 11B neurons, which are the sibling neurons of 11A neurons (Lacin and Truman, 2016; Lacin et al., 2019; Figure 4I).
evidence: This is based on multiple lines of evidence including location, projection patterns, and marker expression shown in Figure 4D,F-I.

claim: 92% of transformed 11A neurons in unc-4 mutants expressed gad1 mRNA, 2% expressed ChAT mRNA, and none co-expressed both.
source: To test whether the transformed 11A neurons in the unc-4 mutants are purely GABAergic or exhibit mixed GABAergic/cholinergic identity, we assayed them for the presence of ChAT and gad1 mRNA (Figure 4J) and found that 92 +/- 5% expressed gad1 mRNA, 2 +/- 4% expressed ChAT mRNA, and none co-expressed both (N = 93 cells, 5 CNSs).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Most transformed 11A neurons switch from a cholinergic to a GABAergic fate in unc-4 mutants.
source: Thus, most of these 11A neurons switch from a cholinergic to a GABAergic fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA in situ hybridization data showing gad1 expression and lack of ChAT expression.

claim: Most converted 11A neurons show GABA production as well as the gad1 mRNA.
source: Moreover, most of these converted neurons show GABA production as well as the gad1 mRNA (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by GABA immunoreactivity data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Unc-4 acts in 11A hemilineage to promote the cholinergic fate and repress the GABAergic fate.
source: Unc-4, thus, appears to act in 11A hemilineage to promote the cholinergic fate and repress the GABAergic fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurotransmitter fate switch observed in 11A neurons in unc-4 mutants.

claim: Misexpression of Unc-4 in immature GABAergic VNC lineages 13A and 19A throughout development did not alter their GABAergic fate.
source: Importantly, misexpression of Unc-4 in immature neurons GABAergic VNC lineages, such as 13A and 19A, throughout development did not, however, alter their GABAergic fate.
evidence: This is an observation from misexpression experiments.

claim: Unc-4 is not a general repressor of the GABAergic fate.
source: Consequently, Unc-4 is not a general repressor of the GABAergic fate (N = 5 animals; not shown).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the misexpression experiments showing lineage-specific effects.

claim: 11A neurons likely function in take-off behavior of flies.
source: 11A neurons likely function in take-off behavior of flies (Harris et al., 2015; Kennedy and Broadie, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Harris et al., 2015 and Kennedy and Broadie, 2018.

claim: The loss of Unc-4 function had no gross defect on neuronal projections with the notable exception of hemilineage 7B.
source: The loss of Unc-4 function had no gross defect on neuronal projections with the notable exception of hemilineage 7B.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from imaging multiple hemilineages shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: 7B neurons exhibited altered projections into the leg neuropils in the absence of Unc-4 function.
source: These neurons exhibited altered projections into the leg neuropils in the absence of Unc-4 function (Figure 5A; see below).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Many 7B neurons in T2 send ipsilateral projection to the T2 leg neuropil.
source: Using multicolor flip-out clones in wild-type animals (Nern et al., 2015), we found that many 7B neurons in T2 send ipsilateral projection to the T2 leg neuropil, others project into all of the contralateral leg neuropils, and others do not innervate the leg neuropil at all (Figure 6A; not shown).
evidence: This is supported by MCFO clone data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Some 7B neurons in T2 project into all of the contralateral leg neuropils.
source: Using multicolor flip-out clones in wild-type animals (Nern et al., 2015), we found that many 7B neurons in T2 send ipsilateral projection to the T2 leg neuropil, others project into all of the contralateral leg neuropils, and others do not innervate the leg neuropil at all (Figure 6A; not shown).
evidence: This is supported by MCFO clone analysis.

claim: Some 7B neurons in T2 do not innervate the leg neuropil at all.
source: Using multicolor flip-out clones in wild-type animals (Nern et al., 2015), we found that many 7B neurons in T2 send ipsilateral projection to the T2 leg neuropil, others project into all of the contralateral leg neuropils, and others do not innervate the leg neuropil at all (Figure 6A; not shown).
evidence: This is supported by MCFO clone analysis.

claim: The projections of 7B neurons into the ipsilateral leg neuropil have synaptic output sites.
source: Of note, we found that the projections of 7B neurons into the ipsilateral leg neuropil have synaptic output sites, indicating that they communicate to other neurons to execute leg-related behaviors (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by synaptotagmin-HA labeling data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 7B neurons communicate to other neurons to execute leg-related behaviors.
source: Of note, we found that the projections of 7B neurons into the ipsilateral leg neuropil have synaptic output sites, indicating that they communicate to other neurons to execute leg-related behaviors (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of synaptic output sites in leg neuropil shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Loss of unc-4 severely reduced 7B projections into the ipsilateral leg neuropils and also reduced contralateral leg projections.
source: All three gave the same result: loss of unc-4 severely reduced 7B projections into the ipsilateral leg neuropils and also reduced contralateral leg projections (Figure 6C–I).
evidence: This is supported by multiple imaging approaches shown in Figure 6C-I.

claim: Unc-4 functions cell autonomously in 7B neurons to support their proper innervation of the leg neuropil.
source: Unc-4, therefore, functions cell autonomously in 7B neurons to support their proper innervation of the leg neuropil.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MARCM and other cell-autonomous manipulation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Previous work showed that activation of 7B neurons elicits take-off behavior in decapitated flies.
source: Previous work showed that activation of 7B neurons elicits take-off behavior in decapitated flies (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2015.

claim: Control animals responded to vial banging stimulus by exhibiting a take-off behavior.
source: Control animals responded to this stimulus by exhibiting a take-off behavior.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations shown in Video 13.

claim: 7B specific Unc-4 knock-out flies raised their wings in an apparent attempt to take off, but they failed to be airborne.
source: In contrast, 7B specific Unc-4 knock-out flies raised their wings in an apparent attempt to take off, but they failed to be airborne.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations shown in Video 13.

claim: 7B specific Unc-4 knock-out flies process the visual stimulus and initiate the take-off behavior by adjusting their posture and raising their wings, but fail to extend their middle legs to cause lift off.
source: This analysis revealed that 7B specific Unc-4 knock-out flies process the visual stimulus, initiate the take-off behavior by adjusting their posture and raising their wings, but fail to extend their middle legs to cause lift off (Figure 7B,C; Video 14).
evidence: This is supported by high-speed video analysis shown in Figure 7B,C and Video 14.

claim: Some 7B specific Unc-4 knock-out flies initiated the flight by just wing flapping without any clear jump.
source: Interestingly, some of these flies initiated the flight by just wing flapping without any clear jump (Video 15).
evidence: This is an observation from high-speed video analysis shown in Video 15.

claim: Hemilineage 7B specific removal of Unc-4 impairs take-off behavior.
source: These results demonstrate that hemilineage 7B specific removal of Unc-4 impairs take-off behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral experiments with 7B-specific Unc-4 knockout.

claim: Animals with ablated 7B neurons behaved essentially identical to 7B specific unc-4 mutants.
source: We investigated whether the observed take-off phenotype was due to the gain of a novel function for the 7B neurons by ablating them during development via expressing the apoptotic gene, head involution defective (hid) in NB3-2 (Bergmann et al., 1998). The resulting animals behaved essentially identical as 7B specific unc-4 mutants (Video 16), indicating the impairment take-off behavior is due to the loss of 7B neuronal function.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral comparison shown in Video 16.

claim: The impairment of take-off behavior in 7B specific unc-4 mutants is due to the loss of 7B neuronal function.
source: We investigated whether the observed take-off phenotype was due to the gain of a novel function for the 7B neurons by ablating them during development via expressing the apoptotic gene, head involution defective (hid) in NB3-2 (Bergmann et al., 1998). The resulting animals behaved essentially identical as 7B specific unc-4 mutants (Video 16), indicating the impairment take-off behavior is due to the loss of 7B neuronal function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of 7B ablation and 7B-specific unc-4 knockout phenotypes.

claim: Unc-4 acts in 7B neurons to promote their leg neuropil innervation, connections that are required for flies to use their legs properly during take-off.
source: Based on our findings, we conclude that Unc-4 acts in 7B neurons to promote their leg neuropil innervation, connections that are required for flies to use their legs properly during take-off.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical and behavioral data on 7B neurons.

claim: All Unc-4+ hemilineages in the adult VNC except the 23B hemilineage heavily innervate the dorsal neuropils of the VNC.
source: All Unc-4+ hemilineages in the adult VNC except the 23B hemilineage heavily innervate the dorsal neuropils of the VNC, which are responsible for flight motor control and wing/haltere related behaviors, including wing-leg coordination (Harris et al., 2015; Namiki et al., 2018; Shepherd et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Harris et al., 2015; Namiki et al., 2018; Shepherd et al., 2019).

claim: Dorsal neuropils of the VNC are responsible for flight motor control and wing/haltere related behaviors, including wing-leg coordination.
source: All Unc-4+ hemilineages in the adult VNC except the 23B hemilineage heavily innervate the dorsal neuropils of the VNC, which are responsible for flight motor control and wing/haltere related behaviors, including wing-leg coordination (Harris et al., 2015; Namiki et al., 2018; Shepherd et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Harris et al., 2015; Namiki et al., 2018; Shepherd et al., 2019).

claim: Hemilineages 7B, 11A, and 18B regulate flight take-off behavior.
source: For example, hemilineages 7B, 11A, and 18B regulate flight take-off behavior and 12A neurons control wing-based courtship singing (Harris et al., 2015; Shirangi et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Harris et al., 2015 and Shirangi et al., 2016.

claim: 12A neurons control wing-based courtship singing.
source: For example, hemilineages 7B, 11A, and 18B regulate flight take-off behavior and 12A neurons control wing-based courtship singing (Harris et al., 2015; Shirangi et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Harris et al., 2015 and Shirangi et al., 2016.

claim: Most Unc-4+ motor neurons are involved with flight, including MN1-5 which innervate the indirect flight muscles, as well as motor neurons that innervate the haltere and neck muscles.
source: In addition, most Unc-4+ motor neurons are also involved with flight – these include MN1-5, which innervate the indirect flight muscles, as well as motor neurons that innervate the haltere and neck muscles, which provide flight stabilization (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on anatomical identification and known functions of these motor neurons, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Haltere and neck muscles provide flight stabilization.
source: In addition, most Unc-4+ motor neurons are also involved with flight – these include MN1-5, which innervate the indirect flight muscles, as well as motor neurons that innervate the haltere and neck muscles, which provide flight stabilization (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of these muscles in flight.

claim: The adult fly VNC is composed of 34 segmentally repeated hemilineages.
source: The adult fly VNC is composed of 34 segmentally repeated hemilineages, which are groups of lineally related neurons with similar features for example, axonal projection and neurotransmitter expression (Truman et al., 2004; Truman et al., 2010; Lacin et al., 2014; Harris et al., 2015; Lacin and Truman, 2016; Shepherd et al., 2016; Lacin et al., 2019; Shepherd et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work including authors' own publications.

claim: Hemilineages are groups of lineally related neurons with similar features such as axonal projection and neurotransmitter expression.
source: The adult fly VNC is composed of 34 segmentally repeated hemilineages, which are groups of lineally related neurons with similar features for example, axonal projection and neurotransmitter expression (Truman et al., 2004; Truman et al., 2010; Lacin et al., 2014; Harris et al., 2015; Lacin and Truman, 2016; Shepherd et al., 2016; Lacin et al., 2019; Shepherd et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Hemilineages function as modular units, each unit appears responsible for regulating particular behaviors.
source: These hemilineages also appear to function as modular units, each unit appears responsible for regulating particular behaviors, indicating the VNC is assembled via a lineage-based functional organization (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2015.

claim: The VNC is assembled via a lineage-based functional organization.
source: These hemilineages also appear to function as modular units, each unit appears responsible for regulating particular behaviors, indicating the VNC is assembled via a lineage-based functional organization (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modular organization of hemilineages, supported by citation to Harris et al., 2015.

claim: The vertebrate spinal cord exhibits lineage-based organization similar to the insect VNC.
source: The vertebrate spinal cord exhibits similar organization: lineally-related neurons acquire similar fates ('cardinal classes') and function in the same or parallel circuits (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2015.

claim: In vertebrate spinal cord, lineally-related neurons acquire similar fates ('cardinal classes') and function in the same or parallel circuits.
source: The vertebrate spinal cord exhibits similar organization: lineally-related neurons acquire similar fates ('cardinal classes') and function in the same or parallel circuits (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2015.

claim: Motor neuron identity in both flies and vertebrates use the same set of transcription factors: Nkx6, Isl, and Lim3.
source: For example, motor neuron identity in both flies and vertebrates, use the same set of transcription factors: Nkx6, Isl, and Lim3 (Tsuchida et al., 1994; Pfaff et al., 1996; Thor and Thomas, 1997; Sander et al., 2000; Broihier and Skeath, 2002; Broihier et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Homologs of many transcription factors expressed in fly VNC interneurons, such as Eve and Lim1, also function in interneurons of the vertebrate spinal cord.
source: Moreover, homologs of many transcription factors expressed in fly VNC interneurons, such as Eve and Lim1, also function in interneurons of the vertebrate spinal cord (Lilly et al., 1999; Moran-Rivard et al., 2001; Pillai et al., 2007; Heckscher et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Unc-4 is expressed in clusters of neurons in the adult VNC and brain.
source: Unc-4 is expressed in clusters of neurons in the adult VNC (E, E') and brain (F).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1E,E',F.

claim: Unc-4 is expressed in the midgut enteroendocrine cells.
source: Unc-4 is expressed in the midgut enteroendocrine cells.
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Unc-4 is expressed in sensory neurons of female and male reproductive tracts.
source: Unc-4 is expressed in sensory neurons of female (H) and male (I) reproductive tracts (arrowheads) in addition to ejaculatory bulb of males (arrow).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H,I.

claim: Unc-4 expression marks bristle sensory neurons in the anterior compartment of the leg but not the ones in the posterior compartment.
source: Unc-4 expression marks bristles sensory neurons in the anterior compartment of the leg but not the ones in the posterior compartment (G).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.
